1086.title: Amen (CCC 1061–1065)
1086.hook: the Creed ends as scripture does: Amen, Christ himself is the Amen
1086.howItsDone: Catholics say amen at the end of the Creed, after prayers at Mass, and when receiving Communion, when the minister says "the Body of Christ" and each person answers amen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new heaven and earth: creation renewed, not thrown away. Your line was all things new. Today, the last word of the Creed.

"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." That's the last verse of the Bible in the Douay-Rheims, and its last word is the one the Creed ends on too. The Creed opens with I believe and travels a long way: God, Christ, the Spirit, the Church, forgiveness, the resurrection, life everlasting. Then a whole church closes it with that small word. For days now, this path has walked through the first part of the Catechism, what Catholics believe. The Catechism closes that part the way the Creed does.
screen: `THE BIBLE'S LAST WORD.` → `I BELIEVE … AMEN.` → `ONE SMALL WORD.`

segments.voice: The Great Amen at Mass came up on day one hundred fifteen; today, the word itself. First, what it is. In Hebrew, the Catechism explains, amen shares its root with the word for believing. It carries the sense of something solid, trustworthy, faithful, something you can lean your weight on. So amen isn't just I agree. It's this holds. Second, God first. In the prophet Isaiah, God himself is called the God of truth, which in Hebrew is the God of amen. People can say amen to God's promises because God is faithful first. Third, a bookend. The Creed's last word, the Catechism says, repeats and confirms its first: I believe. It quotes Saint Augustine, who told new Christians to let the Creed be a kind of mirror, something to look into every day to see whether they still believe what they say. Fourth, the Amen has a name. In the Apocalypse, Christ introduces himself to a church like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness." Not someone who says amen. The Amen. Saint Paul writes that all God's promises find their yes in Christ. In Catholic belief, Christ is God's final, faithful yes to the world, and when people say amen, they join their small yes to his. So the word at the end of the Creed isn't a full stop. It's a signature: everything above this line, I'm leaning my weight on it.
screen: `SOLID, TRUSTWORTHY, FAITHFUL.` · `THE GOD OF AMEN.` · `I BELIEVE … AMEN.` · `THESE THINGS SAITH THE AMEN.`

segments.voice: Breathe in, and on the way out say the word quietly, or in your head, stretched long: amen. Say it again, and this time let it mean what the Catechism says it means: this holds. If you pray, say it to God about something you trust him with; if you don't, let it be a yes to something true in your life, a person, a promise, a place that has held you up.
Amen. A Hebrew word for what is solid and faithful, the last word of the Creed, and, in the Apocalypse, a name for Christ himself. Today's word.
Your line: so be it. A small word that can hold a whole life's weight. See you tomorrow.

1087.title: Liturgy (CCC 1066–1070)
1087.hook: liturgy means the work of the people, now the work of God among us
1087.howItsDone: At Mass Catholics take part through spoken responses, singing, standing, sitting and kneeling together, and in roles such as reader, server, cantor and minister of Communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amen: the Creed's last word, and in the Apocalypse a name for Christ. Your line was so be it. Today, the second part of the Catechism begins.

Stand at the back of a Catholic church during Mass and just listen. The priest says a line, and the whole room answers. He prays, and the room says amen. People stand, sit, kneel, sing, walk forward, go quiet, all together, with hardly anyone giving directions out loud. To a visitor it can look like a show with an audience that happens to know the script. The Catechism paints a picture with no audience in it at all. Its first part was about what Catholics believe. Its second part is about how they celebrate it, and it opens with one word.
screen: `THE ROOM ANSWERS.` → `NOBODY GIVES DIRECTIONS.` → `NOT A SHOW.`

segments.voice: The word is liturgy. Back on day seven hundred ninety-one, this path met the Council's call to take part; now, the word underneath. First, where it comes from. The word originally meant a public work, the Catechism explains, a service done in the name of the people, or on their behalf. Not a private hobby. Second, what the Church did with it. In Christian use, liturgy means the people of God taking part in the work of God. And that work is big: through the liturgy, Catholics believe, Christ himself keeps carrying on the work of saving the world, in his Church, with his Church, and through his Church. The people's work and God's work end up being the same work, done together. Third, it's wider than one room. The New Testament uses this word for Zechariah serving in the Temple, in Luke's Gospel. For preaching the Gospel. And for practical help, like the care one church sent to Paul through a messenger. Worship, preaching, charity: all of it, liturgy. Fourth, the people have a part. The Second Vatican Council asked for the faithful to take part fully, consciously and actively. That's one reason the room answers. When the priest says the Lord be with you, the reply isn't politeness. It's the people doing their part of the work. So there's no audience at Mass. Everyone in the room has a job.
screen: `A PUBLIC WORK.` · `THE PEOPLE IN THE WORK OF GOD.` · `WORSHIP, PREACHING, CHARITY.` · `NO AUDIENCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next shared moment you'll be part of: a Mass, a service, a family meal, a birthday song. Pick one way you'll take part fully instead of watching: answer out loud, sing instead of mouthing, put the phone away. If you pray, offer it ahead of time; if you don't, simply plan to show up all the way.
Liturgy. Once a public work done for the people. For Catholics, the people of God taking part in the work of God, with no one in the room just watching. Today's word.
Your line: the people's work. No one in the room is just watching. Until tomorrow.

1088.title: The whole Christ celebrates (CCC 1136–1144)
1088.hook: heaven and earth, priest and people, all take part
1088.howItsDone: At Mass Catholics sing or say the Holy, holy, holy after the preface, near the start of the Eucharistic Prayer, which the Church understands as joining the praise of the angels and saints in heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, liturgy: once a public work, now the people taking part in the work of God. Your line was the people's work.

A weekday morning Mass in a big church that's mostly empty. A priest at the altar. A woman in the front pew with a worn prayer book. A man near the back who came in on his way to work and kept his coat on. A teenager doing the readings, a little too fast. Rows and rows of empty wood. It looks like a small gathering. The Catechism sees something else: in its picture, that room is packed.
screen: `A MOSTLY EMPTY CHURCH.` → `A FEW PEOPLE, ROWS OF WOOD.` → `THE ROOM IS PACKED.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says the liturgy is the action of the whole Christ. It even gives the Latin, Christus totus: Christ the head, and his body, the Church, together. So who's there? First, heaven. In the Apocalypse, John is shown worship already going on in heaven: a throne, a Lamb "standing as it were slain," angels, elders, and every creature praising God. The living creatures there never stop saying, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come." When the Church celebrates on earth, the Catechism teaches, it joins that heavenly liturgy, already in progress. At Mass, as the great prayer over the bread and wine gets under way, the people sing holy, holy, holy, words close to what the angels sing in the prophet Isaiah. Second, the saints: Mary, the apostles, the martyrs and a great crowd of saints take part. Third, the whole community on earth. It's not the priest alone who celebrates, the Catechism says, but the whole body of Christ, united with its head. Every baptized person shares in it. Fourth, each in their own role. The ordained priest acts in a particular way, in the person of Christ. But readers, servers and singers all have a real part, and all of it is one act. So, back to that weekday morning: a priest, a woman with a prayer book, a man in a coat, a nervous reader, and, in the Catholic understanding, angels, saints and the whole Church. Not a small gathering. A full house.
screen: `CHRISTUS TOTUS: HEAD AND BODY.` · `HEAVEN, ALREADY IN PROGRESS.` · `THE SAINTS AND THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `EACH IN THEIR OWN ROLE.`

segments.voice: Let the room around you get bigger in your mind: somewhere right now, people are gathered to pray, in big churches and small chapels, in hospitals, in kitchens. If you pray, join them slowly with the angels' words from Isaiah, holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, knowing you aren't saying them alone. If you don't, simply sit with the thought that others, somewhere, are reaching toward something larger than themselves.
The whole Christ celebrates. Catholics believe the liturgy is the act of Christ and his whole body: heaven and earth, priest and people, angels and saints, all taking part. Today's word.
Your line: all of us. Head and body, heaven and earth, together. See you tomorrow.

1089.title: Signs and symbols (CCC 1145–1152)
1089.hook: water, oil, bread, wine, light: creation speaks
1089.howItsDone: In the sacraments Catholics use water in baptism, oil in confirmation and anointing, bread and wine at Mass, and candles at baptisms, funerals and the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole Christ celebrates: heaven and earth, priest and people, all at one liturgy. Your line was all of us.

Could a faith get by on ideas alone, with nothing to touch? The Catholic Church doesn't try. At its most solemn moments, it reaches for things any household keeps. Water poured over a baby's head. Oil traced on a forehead. Bread and wine on an altar. A candle burning beside a coffin. Holiness, carried by plain stuff. The Catechism's explanation begins where this path went earlier, with body and soul as one person.
screen: `IDEAS ALONE?` → `WATER, OIL, BREAD, A FLAME.` → `IT BEGINS WITH THE BODY.`

segments.voice: First, people need signs. Human beings are body and spirit together, the Catechism says, so they take in and express spiritual things through physical ones. A hug says more than a memo. A ring says something a contract can't. Second, creation already speaks. God talks to people through the visible world: light and darkness, wind and fire, water and earth, the tree and its fruit. A psalm this path prayed on day one hundred sixty-one says it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands." So when the Church uses water or light, it isn't inventing a code. It's picking up a language creation was already speaking. Third, Israel's covenant with God gave these things a history: anointing kings and priests, laying on hands, sacrifice, and above all the Passover. Bread and wine and oil carried memories long before the Church used them. Fourth, Jesus used them too. In John's Gospel he meets a man born blind, spits on the ground, makes a little mud, spreads it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. The man comes back seeing. The Catechism says Jesus gave ordinary things a new meaning, and that since Pentecost, the Holy Spirit works through the Church's signs, the sacraments, to make people holy. So the bread on your counter and the bread on the altar are not the same in Catholic belief. But the one on your counter isn't nothing either. It's part of the same language.
screen: `BODY AND SPIRIT NEED SIGNS.` · `THE HEAVENS SHEW FORTH.` · `SIGNS OF THE COVENANT.` · `MUD ON A BLIND MAN'S EYES.`

segments.voice: If there's bread nearby, or a glass of water, or anything you'll eat or drink today, hold it and look at it the way you'd look at a gift. Think about where it came from: the field, the rain, the hands that made it and moved it. If you pray, give thanks before you eat it; if you don't, simply let yourself be grateful, and then eat or drink slowly, as if it meant something.
Signs and symbols. Water, oil, bread, wine and light, taken from creation, carried by Israel's covenant, used by Jesus, and in the sacraments, Catholics believe, used by the Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: creation speaks. The Church didn't invent the language; it picked it up. Until tomorrow.

1090.title: Words, song and images (CCC 1153–1162)
1090.hook: the one who sings prays twice, as the saying goes
1090.howItsDone: At Mass Catholics hear scripture read aloud, sing psalms and hymns, and pray in churches decorated with images of Christ, Mary and the saints; Eastern Catholics venerate icons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs and symbols: water, oil, bread, wine and light. Your line was creation speaks.

The one who sings prays twice. That's an old saying as the Catechism gives it, and it credits the line to Saint Augustine. A sentence spoken once is easy to lose by lunch. A sentence sung tends to stay, sometimes for years, attached to a tune that comes back at a red light or in the shower. Yesterday, things: water, oil and bread. Today, the other material of the liturgy: words spoken, words sung, and pictures on the walls.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SINGS PRAYS TWICE.` → `A SUNG LINE STAYS.` → `WORDS, SONG, PICTURES.`

segments.voice: First, words. The Catechism describes the liturgy as a meeting, a conversation between God and his people, carried by actions and words together. That's why every sacrament comes with words: the water of baptism is poured while words are said. The Word of God is read aloud, and the Catechism says the books, the place of reading, the way it's read and the listening all matter. Second, song. Saint Paul tells the Ephesians to speak to one another "in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord." The Catechism sets that beside the saying about praying twice, and beside a story from Augustine's own life. In the days of his baptism in Milan, he heard the church's hymns and wept. The voices flowed into his ears, he wrote, and the truth into his heart. The Church's music, the Catechism says, should be beautiful, help people pray, and let the whole gathering join in, not just the choir. Third, images. The invisible God can't be pictured. But in Jesus, Catholics believe, God became flesh and could be seen. So an image of Christ isn't a guess at the invisible; it points to someone who was really seen. Day seven hundred sixty heard John of Damascus make this case. The Church honors images of Christ, Mary, the angels and the saints, and the honor, the Catechism says elsewhere, passes through the picture to the one pictured. Fourth, they work together: ear, voice and eye, all saying one thing. Some people are moved by an argument. Augustine, by his own account, was moved to tears by a hymn.
screen: `A CONVERSATION OF WORDS AND ACTIONS.` · `PSALMS, AND HYMNS, AND SPIRITUAL CANTICLES.` · `AUGUSTINE WEPT AT THE HYMNS.` · `GOD BECAME FLESH, AND COULD BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Let one song come back to you: a hymn, a carol, a psalm, something sung at a wedding or a funeral or a school assembly long ago. Find one line and sing it softly, out loud if you can, under your breath if you can't. If you pray, let the line be your prayer; if you don't, let it be a way of remembering the people you once sang it with.
Words. In the liturgy, words spoken and sung carry the meeting between God and his people, together with actions and images that point to Christ. Today's word.
Your line: sing it. A sung line tends to stay, sometimes for years. See you tomorrow.

1091.title: Sacred time (CCC 1163–1173)
1091.hook: Sunday and the year make time holy
1091.howItsDone: Catholics gather for Mass on Sundays and holy days, and follow the liturgical year's seasons, Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter and Ordinary Time, marked by readings and the colors of the priest's vestments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, words, song and images, and the one who sings prays twice. Your line was sing it.

A life can run on several calendars at once. Work time, with its deadlines. School time, with its terms. Money time, with its paydays. Sports time, with its seasons and finals. The Catholic Church keeps another calendar running underneath them all. Its week has a center. Its year has seasons with their own colors, purple, white, green, red, on the priest's vestments and the cloth on the altar. A family can go a long while without noticing it. The calendar keeps turning anyway.
screen: `WORK, SCHOOL, MONEY, SPORTS.` → `ANOTHER CALENDAR UNDERNEATH.` → `PURPLE, WHITE, GREEN, RED.`

segments.voice: Day one hundred forty-three gave the colors; today, what the calendar is for. First, the week has a center: Sunday. The Catechism calls it the Lord's Day, the day Christ rose. John uses the same name in the Apocalypse, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." Sunday is both the first day of the week, the day creation began, and the eighth day, beyond the ordinary week, a sign of the new creation. It's when Catholics gather for Mass, a kind of weekly Easter. Second, the year has a heart: Easter. The Catechism calls it the feast of feasts, and quotes Saint Athanasius, who called it the Great Sunday. The light of the Easter days, it says, fills the whole year that follows. Third, the year tells the whole story. Around Easter, the Church walks through Christ's life: waiting in Advent, his birth at Christmas, his appearing to the nations, Lent's long walk toward the cross, and the weeks of Easter. Alongside, it keeps feasts of Mary and memories of martyrs and saints, people who show Christ's Easter at work in real lives. Fourth, the word today. The liturgy keeps saying it: today Christ is born, today he is risen. Not as if it's happening again, but because, Catholics believe, God's saving work isn't trapped in the past. A psalm sung at Easter says it: "This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein." Sacred time is ordinary time, every day of it, given a shape and a center.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE LORD'S DAY.` · `EASTER, THE FEAST OF FEASTS.` · `THE YEAR TELLS THE STORY.` · `THIS IS THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Ask where today sits in the Church's year: Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, or the long stretch the Church calls Ordinary Time. Let the question itself slow you down, because today is not just a Tuesday or a Friday, it's one day in a story with a shape. If you pray, offer this day to God; if you don't, simply notice it as a day that won't come again.
Sacred time. Sunday, the Lord's Day, at the center of the week, and Easter, the feast of feasts, at the heart of the year, giving every ordinary day a shape. Today's word.
Your line: time made holy. Every ordinary day has a place in the story. Same time tomorrow.

1092.title: The church building (CCC 1179–1186)
1092.hook: altar, ambo, font, tabernacle, confessional: each place has a meaning
1092.howItsDone: Catholic churches are arranged around the altar, with an ambo for the readings, a tabernacle for the reserved Eucharist, a font for baptism and a place for confession; some parishes keep the church open for quiet prayer during the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacred time: Sunday and the seasons, the calendar itself made holy. Your line was time made holy.

Why is that there? Ask it of almost anything in a Catholic church. Why is the water by the door? Why does a table of stone or wood stand at the center? Why are the readings proclaimed from one fixed stand? Why does a lamp burn beside one locked cabinet? None of it is there by accident. Each piece has a job, and today's word is the piece whose name is easiest to miss: the reading stand.
screen: `WHY IS THAT THERE?` → `WATER, TABLE, STAND, LAMP.` → `EVERY PIECE HAS A JOB.`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins somewhere surprising: worship in spirit and truth isn't tied to any one place. The people themselves are the Church, built up like living stones, as the first letter of Peter puts it. So why buildings? Because people gather, and a gathering needs a home. A church, the Catechism says, is a house of prayer, where the Eucharist is celebrated and kept, and where the faithful come together. A psalm has the mood of it, in the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." Then it walks through the room. The altar at the center is the altar of sacrifice, and also the table of the Lord, where the people are fed. The tabernacle, which this path visited on day one hundred thirty-eight, keeps the Eucharist after Mass, for the sick and for prayer, in a place of honor. The chair is where the priest presides. And the ambo, today's word, is where the word of God is proclaimed. The Catechism asks for a fitting place for it, so that during the readings everyone's attention turns that way. Church documents speak of two tables at Mass, the table of the word and the table of the Eucharist; the ambo is the first. Then the font, where new Christians are baptized, and a place for the sacrament of penance. The list ends with something that isn't furniture: a church should invite silence and prayer. Even the doorway carries meaning: stepping in is pictured as crossing from a world wounded by sin toward the new life Christ promises.
screen: `WORSHIP ISN'T TIED TO ONE PLACE.` · `ALTAR, TABERNACLE, CHAIR.` · `THE AMBO: THE TABLE OF THE WORD.` · `FONT, CONFESSION, SILENCE, DOOR.` · then, large: `WE SHALL GO INTO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If you're near a church, step in, find the reading stand, then the water, and notice how far apart they are. If not, close your eyes and walk through one you know: door, font, aisle, ambo, altar, the lamp by the tabernacle, one slow breath for each. If you pray, rest in each place for a moment; if you don't, just look.
Ambo. The raised place in a church from which the word of God is proclaimed, the table of the word beside the table of the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: each place speaks. The week went from amen all the way to the room itself. Until tomorrow.
